title: COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHIC STUDY OF THE COMMON COLD
authors: JACK M. GWALTNEY, JR. | C. DOUGLAS PHILLIPS | R. DAVID MILLER | DONALD K. RIKER
key_findings: The common cold is associated with frequent and variable anatomical abnormalities in the upper airways, including occlusion of the ethmoid infundibulum and various sinus cavities. | Functional impairments such as abnormal nasal-airway resistance (94%) and delayed mucosal transport (61%) are highly prevalent during a cold. | Most anatomical and functional abnormalities observed during a cold resolve or significantly improve within two weeks, even without antibiotic treatment, indicating their reversible nature. | The study redefines the common cold as a viral rhinosinusitis, emphasizing the direct or indirect viral causation of sinus abnormalities. | The findings demonstrate a broader anatomical involvement of the upper airway in common colds than previously recognized, enhancing the understanding of its pathogenesis.
conclusion: The common cold is associated with frequent and variable anatomical involvement of the upper airways, including occlusion and abnormalities in the sinus cavities.

title: Common cold
authors: Bruce Arroll | Lauber B | Ball TM | Holberg CJ | Martinez FD | Fry J | Sandler G | Tupasi TE | de Leon LE | Lupisan S | Cruz JR | Pareja G | de Fernandez A | Kvaerner KJ | Nafstad P | Jaakkola JJ | D'Agostino RB Sr | Weintraub M | Russell HK | De Sutter AIM | Lemiengre M | Campbell H | Yoder KE | Shaffer ML | La Tournous SJ | Taverner D | Latte J | Eccles R | Eriksson M | Garreffa S | Kernan WN | Viscoli CM | Brass LM | Kollar C | Schneider H | Waksman J | Kim SY | Chang YJ | Cho HM | Linde K | Fischer P | Melchart D | Shah SA | Sander S | White CM | Mullins RJ | Heddle R | Singh M | Marshall I | Jackson JL | Lesho E | Peterson C | Hulisz D | Kurugol Z | Bayram N | Atik T | Caruso TJ | Prober CG | Gwaltney JM | Jafek BW | Linschoten MR | Murrow BW | D'Cruze H | Kenealy T | Hirt M | Nobel S | Barron E | Mossad SB | Belongia EA | Berg R | Liu K | Douglas RM | Chalker EB | Treacy B | Fahey T | Stocks N | Thomas T | Kaiser L | Lew D | Hirschel B
interventions_studied: analgesics or anti-inflammatory drugs | antibiotics | antihistamines | decongestants for short-term relief | decongestants for long-term relief | decongestants plus antihistamines | echinacea | steam inhalation | vitamin C | zinc (intranasal gel or lozenges)
key_findings: Common cold infections are mostly transmitted through hand-to-hand contact, not droplet spread. Children experience up to 5 colds annually, and adults 2-3, causing discomfort and time off work/school; most symptoms resolve within a week, but coughs often last longer. | Nasal and oral decongestants provide short-term (3-10 hours) relief of nasal congestion, but their long-term effectiveness (>10 hours) is unknown. | Antibiotics are generally ineffective for common cold symptoms, can cause adverse effects, and contribute to antibiotic resistance. They may only be beneficial in specific cases of bacterial co-infection, which are hard to identify. | Vitamin C is unlikely to reduce the duration or severity of cold symptoms. | The effectiveness of zinc gel or lozenges, echinacea, steam inhalation, and analgesics/anti-inflammatory drugs in reducing cold symptom duration is unknown.
conclusion: In this systematic review we present information relating to the effectiveness and safety of the following interventions: analgesics or anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics, antihistamines, decongestants for short-term and for long-term relief, decongestants plus antihistamines, echinacea, steam inhalation, vitamin C, and zinc (intranasal gel or lozenges).

title: Evaluation of echinacea for the prevention and treatment of the common cold: a meta-analysis
authors: Sachin A Shah | Stephen Sander | C Michael White | Mike Rinaldi | Craig I Coleman
interventions_studied: echinacea | Echinaguard | Echinacin | Echinacea angustifolia | Echinacea pallida | Echinacea purpurea | Vitamin C | propolis | Thyme | peppermint | citric acid | Lemongrass leaf | spearmint | rosemary leaf | eucalyptus | fennel seed
key_findings: Echinacea significantly decreased the odds of developing the common cold by 58% (OR 0.42; 95% CI 0.25–0.71). | Echinacea significantly reduced the duration of the common cold by 1.4 days (WMD -1.44, -2.24 to -0.64). | These significant reductions in incidence and duration were maintained across various subgroup and sensitivity analyses, including those for specific echinacea products, concomitant supplement use, and method of cold exposure. | No significant publication bias was detected by the Egger weighted regression statistic for either incidence or duration analyses, despite some asymmetry in funnel plots. | The meta-analysis suggests that echinacea has a benefit in decreasing both the incidence and duration of the common cold, although large-scale prospective studies are still needed.
conclusion: An analysis of the current evidence in the literature suggests that echinacea has a benefit in decreasing the incidence and duration of the common cold; however, large-scale randomised prospective studies controlling for variables such as species, quality of preparation and dose of echinacea, method of cold induction, and objectivity of study endpoints evaluated are needed before echinacea for the prevention or treatment of the common cold can become standard practice.

title: Prevention and treatment of the common cold: making sense of the evidence
interventions_studied: Physical interventions (handwashing, alcohol-based disinfectants, hand-wipes, gloves, masks, gowns) | Zinc (supplement, oral, intranasal, zinc sulfate, zinc gluconate, zinc nasal spray) | Probiotics (Lactobacillus casei, Lactobacillus rhamnosus, other species) | Gargling (water, diluted povidone–iodine solution) | Ginseng (North American ginseng, COLD-FX, Asian ginseng, Ginsana G115) | Exercise | Garlic (Allicin powder) | Homeopathy | Vitamin D | Echinacea (Echinacea purpurea, E. angustifolia) | Vitamin C | Honey | Nasal irrigation (saline drops) | Humidified air | Chinese medicinal herbs | Antihistamine, monotherapy | Antihistamine, combination therapy | Decongestant | Intranasal ipratropium | Over-the-counter cough treatments | Vapour rub | NSAID | Acetaminophen (paracetamol) | Antibiotic | dextromethorphan | codeine | letosteine | brompheniramine–phenylpropanolamine | guaifenesin | pseudophedrine | diphenhydramine | chlorpheniramine | clemastine | Ibuprofen
key_findings: Evidence for interventions aimed at preventing and treating the common cold is frequently of poor quality, and results are inconsistent. | The best evidence for the prevention of the common cold supports physical interventions (e.g., handwashing) and possibly the use of zinc supplements. | The best evidence for traditional treatments supports the use of acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (for pain and fever) and possibly antihistamine-decongestant combinations and intranasal ipratropium. Ibuprofen appears to be superior to acetaminophen for the treatment of fever in children. | The best evidence for nontraditional treatments of the common cold supports the use of oral zinc supplements in adults and honey at bedtime for cough in children over one year.
conclusion: Evidence for interventions aimed at preventing and treating the common cold is frequently of poor quality, and results are inconsistent. The best evidence for prevention supports physical interventions (e.g., handwashing) and possibly zinc supplements. For traditional treatments, acetaminophen and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are supported for pain and fever, with ibuprofen appearing superior to acetaminophen for fever in children. Antihistamine-decongestant combinations and intranasal ipratropium may also be beneficial. For nontraditional treatments, oral zinc supplements in adults and honey at bedtime for cough in children over one year show the best evidence.

title: The common cold: a review of the literature
interventions_studied: monoclonal antibodies against hAPN | Influenza vaccines | antivirals as chemoprophylaxis | Topical application of interferon in the nose | formalin-inactivated whole RSV vaccine | Palizivumab | formalin-inactivated vaccine | recombinant bovine PIV3 attenuated vaccines | human PIV3 attenuated vaccines | bivalent vaccine combination | vaccination | mucosal immunisation | vitamin C | extracts of the plant Echinacea | Zinc | Zinc lozenges | Zinc nasal spray | zinc nasal gel | Alpha agonists | nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug | Nasal decongestants | First-generation antihistamines | ipratropium | cough medications | Intra-nasal interferon | Amantadine | zanamivir | oseltamivir | Ribavarin | Blockade of ICAM-1 cellular receptors | antibiotics
key_findings: The common cold is caused by numerous antigenetically distinct respiratory viruses, with rhinovirus being the most common, and its symptoms arise from both viral cytopathic effects and inflammatory pathways. | Currently, there are no effective therapeutic options for the common cold, making symptomatic management the primary approach, and antibiotics are ineffective and should be avoided. | Rapid and accurate diagnostic techniques, particularly advanced molecular methods, are crucial for guiding appropriate antiviral treatment and preventing the misuse of antibiotics. | The pathogenesis of respiratory viral infections is complex and not fully understood, with different viruses exhibiting varied infection mechanisms and sites of damage within the respiratory tract.
conclusion: The recent discovery of human metapneumovirus and the development of molecular techniques in viral detection represent an exciting time in the study of the common cold. Further research into host inflammatory response and the use of combination therapies may provide a long-term treatment option for this debilitating disease. In the meantime, we as clinicians will have to concentrate on patient education regarding vaccination and avoid unnecessary antibiotic prescription.

title: Understanding the symptoms of the common cold and influenza
interventions_studied: tumour necrosis factor | interferons | interferon beta-1a | pegylated interferon alpha-2b | interferon alpha | indomethacin | acetylsalicylic acid | non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs | anticholinergics | ipratropium | first generation antihistamines
key_findings: Cytokines and inflammatory mediators are primarily responsible for generating the familiar symptoms of common colds and flu, providing physiological explanations for symptoms previously attributed to folklore. | Systemic URTI symptoms (e.g., fever, headache, myalgia, anorexia) are mainly caused by cytokines released from immune cells, while local symptoms (e.g., sore throat, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion) are driven by inflammatory mediators like bradykinin and prostaglandins. | Some unpleasant URTI symptoms, such as fever, malaise, and anorexia, are integral to the acute phase response and may aid in recovery from infection, prompting debate on the benefits of their elimination with symptomatic treatments. | Understanding the pathophysiology of URTI symptoms is crucial because most treatments are symptomatic, and clinical trials for new therapies primarily assess changes in symptom scores.
conclusion: Our understanding of URTI symptoms has improved with the discovery of cytokines and their roles in the acute phase response, providing physiological explanations for symptoms like anorexia previously attributed to folklore. While current URTI treatment focuses on symptom relief, this review suggests that some symptoms, such as fever, malaise, and anorexia, are integral to the acute phase response and may aid recovery. It is debatable whether eliminating these symptoms with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is beneficial, and there is currently no evidence that symptomatic treatment interferes with the course of common cold or influenza, an area warranting further research.

title: Viruses and Bacteria in the Etiology of the Common Cold
authors: MIKA J. MÄKELÄ | TUOMO PUHAKKA | OLLI RUUSKANEN | MAIJA LEINONEN | PEKKA SAIKKU | MARKO KIMPIMÄKI | SOILE BLOMQVIST | TIMO HYYPIÄ | PERTTI ARSTILA
key_findings: Viral etiology was established for 69% of common cold cases in young adults. | Rhinoviruses were the most common cause, accounting for approximately 50% of cases, with outbreaks showing even higher prevalence (up to 92%). | Bacterial infections were rare (found in 7 patients) and most patients, even with serological evidence of bacterial co-infection, recovered without antibiotics. | Advanced diagnostic methods like PCR and serology are crucial for detecting the full spectrum of viral infections, beyond just virus culture. | The specific viral etiology of the common cold can vary significantly based on the epidemiological situation and circulating viruses.
conclusion: In routine clinical practice, there is no need to do etiological diagnosis of the common cold. The price is too high (in this study, $700/patient), and, except in the case of the rapid influenza A test, the results may not change the treatment. The implications of this study, nevertheless, are clear. The common cold is a viral illness for which the etiology can be shown in most cases. Bacterial coinfections are very rare. Antibiotic treatment is not necessary in otherwise healthy young adults with common colds.

title: Vitamin C for Preventing and Treating the Common Cold
key_findings: Prophylactic vitamin C supplementation does not reduce the incidence of common colds in the general population, but it significantly reduces incidence by 50% in individuals exposed to extreme physical stress or cold. | Continuous prophylactic use of vitamin C significantly reduces the duration of common cold episodes, by an average of 14% in children and 8% in adults. | Therapeutic use of vitamin C at the onset of cold symptoms generally shows no benefit in reducing cold duration in adults, with one exception of a single 8g dose reducing duration. | The clinical significance of the minor reduction in cold duration during prophylaxis for the general population is questionable, despite indicating a genuine biological effect.
conclusion: The review concludes that prophylactic vitamin C supplementation does not significantly reduce the incidence of the common cold in normal populations, casting doubt on its widespread utility. While a minor reduction in the duration of cold episodes during prophylaxis was observed, its clinical significance is questionable, despite suggesting a genuine biological effect. However, in special circumstances involving extreme physical exertion and/or cold stress, vitamin C supplementation may offer considerable beneficial effects. Therapeutic use of vitamin C at the onset of symptoms has shown no clear benefits, though further assessment of high-dose single treatments is warranted. The effect of therapeutic vitamin C on children has not yet been examined.
